distractors.C: Path-scoped rules are an excellent fit for conventions keyed to file type and would solve the misapplication cleanly. Emptying `CLAUDE.md` entirely goes too far: genuinely universal standards should be always-loaded, and forcing them into glob-scoped rules means they apply only when a matching file happens to be open.
distractors.D: Per-package `CLAUDE.md` files do scope conventions correctly and are a legitimate part of the hierarchy. Deleting the root file loses the shared universal standards, and conventions common to several packages get duplicated across directories, which reintroduces the maintenance problem in a new form.

scenario: A reviewer objects to the line `@../../docs/standards/graphql.md` in `packages/api/CLAUDE.md`, arguing that pasting the standards inline would be simpler and produce identical behavior. The standards file is also read by humans and is referenced by two other packages.
stem: What is the strongest argument for keeping the import?

options.text: Imports are resolved lazily and are exempt from position effects, since imported content is injected at the start of the loaded context.
The standards stay a single source of truth: one canonical file serves human readers, and all three packages pick up changes automatically.
Imports are resolved lazily, so the standards consume context only when a GraphQL file is being edited.
Inlining would exceed the practical size limit for a package-level `CLAUDE.md`.

rationale.correct: The reviewer is right that the loaded content ends up equivalent — the value of `@import` is maintenance, not behavior. One canonical file serves both human readers and three packages, and updating it propagates everywhere without touching any package's configuration. Inlining creates three copies that drift.

distractors.A: There is no such exemption. Imported content is assembled into the memory file like any other content and is subject to the same position effects.
distractors.C: Conditional loading is a genuine and valuable capability, which is what makes this plausible. It comes from `.claude/rules/` with path globs in the frontmatter, not from `@import` — imports are resolved as part of assembling the memory file, so the content loads regardless of which file is open.
distractors.D: Keeping memory files lean is legitimately good practice and oversized configuration does cause problems. There is no specific size limit being invoked here, and the reviewer's objection is about duplication versus reference rather than about size.

scenario: A `/analyze-schema` skill inspects the database schema and reports inconsistencies. It works, but it emits several thousand tokens of table dumps into the conversation, and developers report that Claude becomes vague about their original task afterward. The skill is in `.claude/skills/` and shared with the team.
stem: What is the most appropriate change?

options.text: Move the skill to `~/.claude/skills/` so its output affects only the developer who invokes it.
Rewrite the skill to summarize the schema itself and emit only the inconsistencies it finds.
Instruct developers to run `/compact` after invoking the skill, clearing the table dumps from context before they continue with their task.
Add `context: fork` to the skill's frontmatter so it runs in an isolated sub-agent context and returns only its findings.

rationale.correct: `context: fork` exists for exactly this: skills that produce verbose intermediate output run in an isolated sub-agent context, so the main conversation receives the result without the noise. It is a one-line frontmatter change and it protects every invocation automatically.

distractors.A: Skill scope controls who can invoke a skill, not how its output interacts with context. Moving it to user scope would deprive the team of a working skill while leaving the verbosity problem exactly as it is for whoever runs it.
distractors.B: Reducing the skill's output at the source is genuinely good design and would help. Some verbosity is inherent to inspecting a schema, and any remaining intermediate reasoning still lands in the main conversation — forking removes the whole class of problem rather than shrinking it.
distractors.C: Running `/compact` afterward does reclaim context and is a reasonable manual remedy. It is reactive, depends on developers remembering, and compaction condenses the original task context too, so some of the vagueness it is meant to fix can survive.

scenario: Your team's shared `/scaffold-service` skill generates a new service directory. You want a personal variant that also wires in your preferred logging library, and you must not change behavior for teammates. You also want the variant restricted to file-write operations so it cannot invoke shell commands, and you want it to hint for the service name when you invoke it bare.
stem: Which configuration satisfies all three requirements?

options.text: Edit the shared skill in `.claude/skills/` to add your logging library behind a flag, and set `allowed-tools` and `argument-hint` in its frontmatter.
Create the variant in `.claude/commands/` as a personal slash command, since commands are not shared the way skills are.
A differently named variant in `~/.claude/skills/`, with `allowed-tools` restricting file operations and `argument-hint` prompting for the service name.
Copy the skill into `~/.claude/skills/` under the same name so it shadows the shared one, and add `context: fork` to isolate its file operations.

rationale.correct: Each requirement maps to one mechanism. A differently named variant in user-scoped `~/.claude/skills/` keeps it personal and avoids colliding with the shared skill. `allowed-tools` in the frontmatter restricts what the skill may do during execution, which is the guard against destructive operations. `argument-hint` prompts for a required parameter when the skill is invoked without arguments.

distractors.A: Adding a flag to the shared skill would work functionally and keeps one implementation. It modifies version-controlled team configuration to serve a personal preference, and the `allowed-tools` restriction you want would then constrain everyone.
distractors.B: Personal slash commands are a real mechanism and would keep this out of the shared skill set, so the instinct is sound. The path given here is the project-scoped commands directory, which is shared via version control — so this variant would reach teammates, violating the one requirement the scenario states most firmly.
distractors.D: Same-name shadowing in user scope is a recognizable pattern from other tools and would keep your muscle memory intact. Using a distinct name is the safer convention precisely because it avoids ambiguity about which skill ran, and `context: fork` isolates conversational context rather than restricting tool access — it is not a safety control.

scenario: You are deciding where two things belong. The first is a naming convention every file in the repository must follow, with no exceptions. The second is a multi-step release-checklist procedure that engineers run a few times per month and that involves roughly 400 lines of instructions.
stem: Where should each go?

options.text: The naming convention in `CLAUDE.md` as an always-loaded standard; the release checklist as an on-demand skill.
The naming convention as a `.claude/rules/` file with a glob matching all source files; the release checklist in `CLAUDE.md` so it is always available.
Both in `CLAUDE.md`, so neither depends on the engineer remembering to invoke anything.
Both as skills, keeping `CLAUDE.md` minimal and loading each only when relevant.

rationale.correct: The split follows from how each is used. A universal, no-exceptions convention must apply to every interaction, which is what always-loaded `CLAUDE.md` content provides. A 400-line procedure needed a few times a month is task-specific and would waste context on every unrelated request, which is exactly what on-demand skill invocation is for.

distractors.B: A rule with a glob covering all source files would enforce the naming convention and is a defensible way to express it. A glob that matches everything is just an always-loaded standard with extra machinery, and the second half inverts the checklist placement — putting 400 lines of occasional procedure into always-loaded context is the costlier error.
distractors.C: Putting both in `CLAUDE.md` guarantees availability, and the instinct to not rely on invocation is reasonable for the convention. It loads 400 lines of release procedure into every conversation regardless of relevance, which crowds out context that the current task needs.
distractors.D: Making both skills keeps `CLAUDE.md` lean, which is a real virtue. A convention with no exceptions cannot depend on someone choosing to invoke it — if it only applies when summoned, it is not universal.

scenario: Your repo has Terraform under `infra/`, React components under `src/components/`, and test files colocated beside the code they test throughout the entire tree (`Button.test.tsx` next to `Button.tsx`, `handler.test.ts` next to `handler.ts`). Each category has distinct conventions. You want the right conventions applied automatically based on what is being edited.
stem: What is the most maintainable configuration?

options.text: `.claude/rules/` files for all three, scoped `paths: ["infra/**/*"]`, `paths: ["src/components/**/*"]`, and `paths: ["**/*.test.*"]`.
A `CLAUDE.md` in each of the three locations, with the test conventions duplicated into every directory containing test files.
A `CLAUDE.md` in `infra/` and one in `src/components/`, plus a `.claude/rules/` file with `paths: ["**/*.test.*"]` for the test conventions.
One `.claude/rules/` file containing all three convention sets, scoped with a combined glob list covering all three patterns.

rationale.correct: All three are conditional convention sets, and expressing them uniformly as path-scoped rules keeps the mechanism consistent and each set independently editable. The glob approach is required for the test conventions, since those files are spread across the tree and cannot be captured by any directory boundary, and it works equally well for the two that happen to be directory-shaped.

distractors.B: Directory-level `CLAUDE.md` cannot express the test conventions without duplicating them into every directory that holds a test file. That is a large and permanent maintenance burden, and the copies will drift as soon as one is updated in isolation.
distractors.C: This is a legitimate hybrid: directory-level `CLAUDE.md` is a real part of the hierarchy and fits conventions that genuinely align to a directory. It splits one concern across two mechanisms, so contributors must know which place to look and which to edit — a maintainability cost the question is asking you to weigh.
distractors.D: A single rules file with a combined glob is compact and does load conditionally. Because any matching path activates the whole file, editing a Terraform file would load the React and test conventions too, which is the irrelevant-context problem path scoping exists to prevent.

scenario: A team adds `.claude/rules/security.md` with `paths: ["src/auth/**/*"]` containing critical rules: never log credentials, always use the constant-time comparison helper. A month later, a developer adds a new authentication flow under `src/api/login/` and Claude generates code that logs the raw password. The rule file is correct and loads properly when editing files under `src/auth/`.
stem: What does this reveal?

options.text: The glob assumed all authentication code lives under `src/auth/`; scoping that gates a critical rule is only as good as that assumption.
The developer should have invoked a security review skill before committing the new flow.
The rules file needs `paths: ["**/*"]` so it loads for every file and cannot be missed.
Path-scoped rules are inherently unreliable for security requirements, and rules this critical should be moved into always-loaded `CLAUDE.md`.

rationale.correct: The mechanism worked exactly as configured; the glob was the defect. Path scoping trades guaranteed loading for reduced irrelevant context, and that trade is only safe when the pattern genuinely covers everywhere the concern arises. Recognizing that a rule's criticality should inform how conservatively it is scoped is the real lesson.

distractors.B: A security review step is a valuable additional control and would likely have caught this. It is a process addition rather than an explanation, and it leaves the mis-scoped rule in place to fail the same way next time.
distractors.C: Widening the glob to everything does guarantee the rule always loads, and for a rule this critical that instinct is defensible. A glob matching all files is an always-loaded rule wearing path-scoping clothing, so it is clearer to express it as such — and it loads security rules into every unrelated edit, which is the cost path scoping exists to avoid.
distractors.D: Moving critical rules to always-loaded configuration is a reasonable conclusion and may well be the right call here. Framing path-scoped rules as inherently unreliable overstates it — they behaved deterministically and correctly; the glob simply did not describe the intended scope.

scenario: A team is deciding between a `CLAUDE.md` inside `src/api/` and a `.claude/rules/` file scoped with `paths: ["src/api/**/*"]` for their API conventions. Today all API code lives under `src/api/`. They anticipate extracting some API handlers into `packages/edge-api/` next quarter.
stem: Which consideration should decide it?

options.text: The directory-level `CLAUDE.md`, because colocating conventions with the code they govern makes them more discoverable to human readers.
Either is equivalent today, so the team should pick based on which format they find easier to write.
The rules file: a glob extends to the new location in one line, while a directory-level file must be duplicated or moved.
The rules file, because directory-level `CLAUDE.md` files are deprecated in favor of `.claude/rules/`.

rationale.correct: Both work identically for the current layout, so the anticipated split is the deciding factor. A glob list extends to `packages/edge-api/**/*` with a one-line edit and keeps a single definition, whereas a directory-bound file must be copied to the new location — creating two copies that drift — or moved, which breaks the original.

distractors.A: Discoverability is a genuine benefit of colocation and matters for human contributors, which makes this a real trade-off rather than a wrong answer. It is outweighed here by the known upcoming split, and discoverability can be recovered with a pointer in the package README.
distractors.B: It is accurate that the two are functionally equivalent for today's layout, which is why this is tempting. The question supplies the future split precisely so it can inform the decision, and ignoring known upcoming change is what produces avoidable rework.
distractors.D: Directory-level `CLAUDE.md` files are a supported part of the configuration hierarchy and are not deprecated. Choosing correctly for a stated reason that is false leaves the team with a wrong model of the tooling.

scenario: A production bug has a clear stack trace pointing at one function in one file. The fix is a null check on a single parameter. A teammate suggests entering plan mode first "because it is safer to plan before changing production code."
stem: How should you respond?

options.text: Use plan mode but skip the exploration phase, going straight to writing the plan so the overhead is minimal.
Use direct execution, but only because the change is small; if it touched two or more files, plan mode would be required regardless of clarity.
Use direct execution: the scope is clear, the location is known, and there are no competing approaches or architectural decisions.
Agree, since any change to production code carries risk and planning reduces it at low cost.

rationale.correct: Plan mode is for large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file work. None applies: the stack trace localizes the defect, the fix is a single well-understood conditional, and there is no design choice to make. Direct execution is the appropriate mode, and using plan mode here is overhead rather than safety.

distractors.A: Plan mode without exploration discards the part that creates the value — surveying the code before committing to an approach. What remains is a formality that delays a change whose shape is already known.
distractors.B: This reaches the right conclusion, which makes it superficially attractive. The stated rule is wrong: file count is not the criterion. A two-file change with an obvious fix still suits direct execution, and a single-file change with several competing designs can genuinely warrant planning.
distractors.D: Caution about production code is reasonable and this reflects a sound instinct. Plan mode's value comes from resolving uncertainty about approach and scope, and neither is uncertain here — so it adds ceremony without reducing the actual risk, which is better handled by tests and review.

scenario: You must migrate a library used in 45 files. Two migration paths exist with different infrastructure requirements. You enter plan mode; the agent begins reading files to map usage, and after roughly 30 files its answers grow inconsistent and it starts referring to "typical patterns" instead of the specific call sites it found earlier.
stem: What is the right adjustment?

options.text: Keep plan mode and use the Explore subagent for discovery, so verbose file-reading stays isolated and the session keeps room to decide.
Split the migration into three plan-mode sessions of 15 files each and merge the resulting plans.
Abandon plan mode and switch to direct execution, migrating file by file so no single session must hold the whole picture.
Keep plan mode and run `/compact` once the agent starts drifting, then continue reading the remaining files.

rationale.correct: The task genuinely warrants plan mode — 45 files and two competing approaches with different infrastructure implications. The problem is that verbose discovery is consuming the context the architectural reasoning needs. The Explore subagent isolates that output and returns summaries, which is precisely the pattern for preventing context exhaustion during multi-phase work.

distractors.B: Partitioning bounds each session's context and is a sensible instinct for large surveys. The choice between the two migration paths depends on the complete usage picture, so plans formed against one-third of the call sites each cannot be merged into a coherent decision.
distractors.C: Direct execution avoids the context problem by never building the full picture, which is why it is tempting. It also forecloses the architectural choice — you would begin migrating before deciding which path to take, which is the rework plan mode exists to prevent.
distractors.D: Compacting does reclaim context and would let the session continue, so it is a reasonable stopgap. It is reactive and lossy: the specific call-site details already gathered get condensed exactly when they are needed for the decision, and the same drift recurs as reading resumes.

scenario: You used plan mode to design a migration and the resulting plan is clear, sequenced, and agreed by the team. Execution involves 45 mechanical edits following the approved approach, with no remaining design questions.
stem: How should you carry out the plan?

options.text: Stay in plan mode throughout execution so each edit is checked against the plan before it is applied.
Start a fresh session for execution without the plan in context, so prior reasoning does not bias the implementation.
Switch to direct execution, since the uncertainty plan mode addressed has been resolved.
Re-enter plan mode before each group of related files, to confirm the plan still holds as the codebase changes.

rationale.correct: Plan mode and direct execution are complementary phases of one task. Planning resolved the questions about approach and scope; what remains is mechanical work against an agreed design. Switching to direct execution for implementation is the intended pairing.

distractors.A: Staying in plan mode sounds disciplined and appeals to a desire for verification at each step. Plan mode exists to explore and design before committing, not to gate individual edits, so using it this way stalls execution without adding meaningful safety.
distractors.B: Discarding prior reasoning is the right move when you want an independent perspective — reviewing generated code, for instance. Here the plan is the thing being implemented, so dropping it from context means executing without the design you just agreed on.
distractors.D: Periodic re-planning is a defensible hedge on a long migration and would catch genuine surprises. It reintroduces planning overhead for a plan the team already agreed to, and if a surprise does surface it will announce itself during execution — at which point re-planning is a response rather than a routine.

scenario: You have asked three times for a data-cleaning function that "normalizes messy customer names." Each attempt interprets it differently: one title-cases everything including `McDonald`, one strips all punctuation including legitimate hyphens, one reorders `Last, First` inconsistently. Your prose description is detailed and has not helped.
stem: What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Write a test suite covering the edge cases first, then iterate by sharing the failures.
Rewrite the prose description with more precision, enumerating each transformation rule explicitly.
Use the interview pattern, having Claude ask questions about the normalization rules before implementing.
Provide two or three concrete input/output pairs so the transformation is specified by example rather than description.

rationale.correct: Prose has now failed three times against the same ambiguity, and concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate an expected transformation when descriptions are interpreted inconsistently. Each pair pins down one contested behavior unambiguously, which is what prose has been unable to do.

distractors.A: Test-driven iteration is a strong technique and would eventually converge, since failures are concrete feedback. It is a heavier loop than needed — the examples that would make good tests can specify the behavior directly, without requiring a generate-fail-share cycle per case.
distractors.B: More precise prose is the obvious next escalation and is what most people reach for. Three detailed attempts have already failed, which is the signal that the medium — not the level of detail — is the constraint.
distractors.C: The interview pattern is genuinely valuable for surfacing considerations you have not thought of, which is the situation where requirements are underexplored. Here you already know what you want; the gap is conveying it, so questioning adds a round trip without addressing the transmission problem.

scenario: A generated migration script has three defects. First, it does not handle null values in the `phone` column. Second, its batch size causes timeouts on large tables. Third, its rollback path assumes the batch size, so changing the batch size also changes what rollback must undo.
stem: How should you communicate these?

options.text: Report the null handling separately, then the batch size and rollback together, since only those two interact.
Report all three in a single detailed message, since the batch size and rollback defects interact.
Report them one at a time in severity order, verifying each fix before moving to the next.
Report all three separately in parallel sessions so each fix is developed without interference from the others.

rationale.correct: Interacting problems should be raised together so the fix accounts for the relationship. Batch size and rollback are explicitly coupled, so addressing them in isolation risks a rollback path that no longer matches the batching. Including the null handling in the same message costs nothing and keeps the script consistent in one revision.

distractors.A: This shows accurate reasoning about which defects interact and applies the right principle, making it the strongest alternative. Splitting into two rounds buys nothing — the independent null fix does not conflict with anything, so separating it adds a round trip without reducing risk.
distractors.C: Sequential iteration is the correct approach for independent problems and is a reasonable default. Two of these are coupled, so fixing batch size first without the rollback constraint in view invites a change that the next round has to partly undo.
distractors.D: Parallel isolated sessions would produce three fixes that were each developed unaware of the others, and merging the coupled pair would require reconciling two incompatible assumptions about batching.

scenario: You need a caching layer for a service in a domain you do not know well. You can describe roughly what you want but suspect there are considerations — invalidation strategy, stampede behavior, failure modes when the cache is unavailable — that you have not thought through.
stem: Which refinement technique fits best?

options.text: Write a test suite covering the behaviors you can think of, then iterate on failures.
Use the interview pattern: have Claude ask questions to surface considerations you have not anticipated before implementing.
Provide input/output examples of cache hits, misses, and expirations to specify the expected behavior precisely before implementation.
Ask for three candidate implementations with different trade-offs and choose among them.

rationale.correct: The stated problem is unknown unknowns in an unfamiliar domain. The interview pattern is designed for exactly that: questions surface design considerations you would not have raised yourself, before implementation locks in assumptions. The scenario even names the kind of issues it would expose.

distractors.A: Test-driven iteration is excellent when you know the target behavior, and it would firm up what you can already articulate. Tests can only cover behaviors you thought of, so the considerations you have not anticipated remain untested and unaddressed.
distractors.C: Input/output examples resolve ambiguity in a transformation you can already describe. Cache invalidation and failure modes are design decisions rather than input/output mappings, so examples cannot express them.
distractors.D: Comparing candidate implementations does expose trade-offs concretely and is a legitimate way to learn a domain. It is more expensive than asking, and it leaves you evaluating options against criteria you have not yet worked out — which is the actual gap.

scenario: Your CI review job runs `claude -p "Review this diff"` and a downstream step posts findings as inline comments on specific files and lines. The parser breaks whenever Claude's prose wording shifts. An engineer proposes a more robust regex parser.
stem: What is the better fix?

options.text: Add a system prompt instructing Claude to always emit findings in the exact format `file:line: message`.
Use `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` to require structured findings with explicit file and line fields.
Harden the regex parser to tolerate the known wording variants and add a fallback that posts a single summary comment when parsing fails.
Add few-shot examples of correctly formatted findings so the output format stays consistent across runs.

rationale.correct: CI needs a stable contract, and the CLI provides one: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` produces structured findings whose shape is enforced rather than requested. File and line become declared fields the downstream step reads directly, so the failure mode of parsing free text disappears entirely.

distractors.A: A format instruction in the prompt is the cheapest change and would raise conformance. It is the same probabilistic approach as few-shot with less signal, and it leaves the pipeline parsing text that the model is merely asked to shape.
distractors.C: A more tolerant parser plus a summary fallback is pragmatic and would reduce breakage, which makes it a real option. It is still parsing unconstrained natural language, so novel phrasings keep appearing, and the fallback silently degrades inline comments to a lump summary — losing the per-line placement that motivated the design.
distractors.D: Few-shot examples do improve format consistency and are the right technique when no structural enforcement is available. They make conformance likely rather than guaranteed, and one non-conforming run in CI breaks the pipeline — a weaker guarantee than schema enforcement when one is on offer.

scenario: Your CI review posts findings on each push. On a PR with six pushes, developers received the same three unaddressed findings six times, generating 18 comments. They have started ignoring the bot. Each CI run invokes Claude Code fresh with only the current diff.
stem: What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Review only the incremental diff since the previous push rather than the full PR diff.
Run the review only once, when the PR is first marked ready for review.
Include the prior review's findings in each subsequent run's context, instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
Deduplicate downstream by hashing each finding's file, line, and message, and suppress any comment already posted on the PR.

rationale.correct: Each run is stateless, so it rediscovers everything and has no way to know what was already said. Feeding prior findings into context and instructing Claude to report only what is new or still unaddressed gives the review the memory it lacks, while keeping full-diff analysis so nothing is missed.

distractors.A: Incremental-diff review reduces repetition and cuts cost, which is genuinely attractive. It also blinds the review to issues introduced earlier in the PR and to regressions where a later push breaks something reviewed clean before, so coverage suffers.
distractors.B: A single review at ready-for-review eliminates duplicates outright and is defensible for small PRs. It gives up continuous feedback, so problems introduced after that point go unreviewed — which is most of what the automation was for.
distractors.D: Downstream deduplication would suppress the repeat comments and is straightforward to implement, making it a solid answer. It is a presentation-layer patch: the model still re-reports resolved and unresolved issues indiscriminately, and exact hashing fails as soon as line numbers shift or wording varies slightly between runs.

scenario: A CI job generates tests for changed modules. The output is voluminous and low value: it asserts framework behavior, re-tests scenarios the existing suite already covers, and builds its own mocks instead of using the project's established fixtures. The job passes only the changed files to Claude Code.
stem: Which combination most improves the output?

options.text: Lower the generation temperature so output is more conservative and less prone to producing redundant tests.
Pass the existing test files in context, and document testing standards, value criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md.
Post-process the generated tests, discarding any whose assertions closely match an existing test.
Add a system prompt instructing Claude to write only high-value tests and to avoid testing framework behavior.

rationale.correct: All three defects come from missing context. The instance cannot avoid duplicating tests it has never seen, and it cannot use fixtures or apply value criteria it was never told about. Supplying the existing tests addresses duplication directly, and CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving a CI-invoked instance the project's standards, criteria, and fixture conventions.

distractors.A: Temperature affects sampling variability, not knowledge. A more deterministic run will duplicate existing tests just as reliably and still will not know the fixtures exist.
distractors.C: Post-hoc filtering would remove some duplicates and is a reasonable safety net. It runs after the tokens are spent, catches only near-identical assertions, and does nothing for the fixture and value problems — so most of the low-value output survives.
distractors.D: A prompt instruction is cheap and would trim the most obvious framework-behavior tests. "High-value" is undefined without the project's criteria, and the instruction does nothing about duplication or fixtures, since those require information the instance does not have.

scenario: Your automated review flags outdated comments with a 60% false positive rate. The current instruction is "check that comments are accurate." An engineer proposes appending "be conservative and only report high-confidence findings."
stem: How should you evaluate that proposal?

options.text: Adopt it, since instructing the model to require higher confidence is the standard way to trade recall for precision.
Adopt it as an interim measure while the comment-checking category is disabled, then remove the wording once explicit criteria have been written.
Reject it and instead have the model emit a numeric confidence score per finding, filtering below a tuned threshold.
Reject it and replace the vague instruction with a specific categorical criterion: flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts the code.

rationale.correct: "Be conservative" and "only high-confidence findings" give the model no new information about which comments are actually problems. Precision comes from a specific categorical rule the model can apply — here, contradiction between claimed and actual behavior — which converts a subjective judgment into a checkable one.

distractors.A: This is the intuitive move and reflects how the trade-off is usually described. General confidence language does not reliably shift the decision boundary because it does not tell the model what distinguishes a real finding from a stylistic quibble, so output volume drops without precision improving proportionally.
distractors.B: Disabling a high-false-positive category to protect developer trust while the prompt is improved is a legitimate tactic and half of this is right. Pairing it with the ineffective instruction wastes the interim period, and the disable already provides the protection the vague instruction was supposed to buy.
distractors.C: Self-reported confidence scores have real uses when calibrated against labeled data, so this is not baseless. Uncalibrated model confidence is a poor proxy — the model is confidently wrong on exactly the cases producing false positives — and this adds filtering machinery instead of fixing an underspecified criterion.

scenario: Your review bot reports across three categories. Security and null-safety findings are accurate and valued. Naming-convention findings are 70% false positives. Developers have begun dismissing all findings without reading them, including security ones. Rewriting the naming criteria properly will take about two weeks.
stem: What should you do in the meantime?

options.text: Keep all four categories running but mark naming findings as low severity so developers can prioritize.
Temporarily disable the naming-convention category so the accurate categories regain trust, re-enabling it once its criteria are rewritten.
Keep all four but post naming findings to a separate low-visibility channel rather than as inline PR comments.
Disable the bot entirely until all three categories have been validated, so developers never learn to distrust a tool that is partly broken.

rationale.correct: The concrete harm is that one bad category is destroying trust in two good ones, and dismissal has already generalized. Temporarily disabling the offending category restores the signal-to-noise ratio immediately and preserves the value of the accurate categories while its criteria are fixed.

distractors.A: Severity labeling is reasonable when findings are accurate but differ in importance. It does not help here, because the problem is correctness rather than priority — a low-severity false positive is still wrong, and the noise remains in the same stream developers have learned to ignore.
distractors.C: Routing noisy findings elsewhere is a genuine improvement over inline comments and preserves the data for tuning, which makes it a strong second choice. The false positives still exist and still consume attention in the other channel, and it requires building and maintaining a second surface to house output you have already judged unreliable.
distractors.D: Refusing to ship a partly broken tool is a defensible standard. It discards two weeks of accurate security and null-safety findings to avoid one bad category, which is a worse outcome than removing the category that is actually causing harm.

scenario: Reviews assign severity inconsistently: the same missing-input-validation pattern is labeled critical in one PR and low in another. The prompt says "assign a severity of critical, high, medium, or low based on the impact of the issue."
stem: What most improves consistency?

options.text: Have the model assign a 1–100 impact score and map score ranges onto the four severity labels.
Reduce the scale to two levels — blocking and non-blocking — so there are fewer boundaries to draw.
Define each severity level with explicit criteria and a concrete code example illustrating what qualifies.
Run each review three times and take the majority severity for each finding.

rationale.correct: "Based on the impact of the issue" leaves every boundary to the model's judgment, which is why the same pattern lands differently across runs. Explicit criteria per level, anchored by a concrete code example, give the model a reference to classify against rather than a subjective scale to interpret.

distractors.A: A numeric score with defined ranges looks more rigorous and makes the mapping explicit. The variance simply relocates into the score itself, since "impact" remains undefined — an uncalibrated 1–100 judgment is less stable than a four-way choice, not more.
distractors.B: Fewer levels does reduce the number of boundaries and would genuinely cut some variance, so this is a reasonable simplification. The remaining boundary is still undefined, so the same input can land on either side of it — and you lose prioritization granularity to buy partial relief.
distractors.D: Majority voting across runs would smooth some inconsistency and is a recognized ensembling technique. It triples cost, still produces arbitrary-but-stable answers where criteria are genuinely undefined, and treats the symptom rather than the missing definition.

scenario: Your extraction prompt handles the three document layouts you supplied few-shot examples for. A fourth layout appears in production — a scanned form with a two-column body — and extraction produces empty required fields. You could add a fourth example for this layout, but new layouts keep appearing.
stem: What is the most durable improvement to the examples?

options.text: Increase the number of examples per known layout from one to three, so each format is more strongly represented.
Replace layout-specific examples with a single example that shows the desired output schema, and rely on the schema to constrain extraction across any layout.
Add one example per new layout as it appears, treating the example set as a growing catalog of known formats.
Choose examples that demonstrate locating a field under structurally different presentations, so the model generalizes rather than pattern-matches.

rationale.correct: Few-shot examples work best when they let the model generalize judgment to novel patterns rather than memorize specific cases. Choosing examples that vary structurally and show how a field is located under each presentation teaches a transferable strategy, which is what a stream of new layouts demands.

distractors.A: More examples per known layout strengthens performance on those layouts and is a standard way to improve consistency. It adds no coverage for unseen formats, so the failure mode described is untouched while token cost rises.
distractors.B: Schema constraints do guarantee the output shape and are essential for structured extraction, so this is half of a good design. A schema specifies what the result must look like, not how to find the values in an unfamiliar layout, and dropping the examples removes the signal that handles structural variety — often producing nulls or fabricated values.
distractors.C: Cataloguing each layout as it appears does fix each case and is a reasonable reactive process. It is permanently one step behind production, grows the prompt without bound, and leaves every genuinely new layout failing on first contact — which the scenario says is a recurring event.

scenario: Your code review flags every use of a bare `except:` clause as a bug. In your codebase, bare excepts inside the retry decorator and the plugin loader are deliberate and documented; everywhere else they are genuine defects. Developers are dismissing the retry and plugin findings each week.
stem: What is the most effective way to reduce these false positives?

options.text: Add path exclusions so the retry decorator and plugin loader files are skipped by the review.
Add a rule to the prompt stating that bare excepts in the retry decorator and plugin loader are acceptable.
Provide few-shot examples contrasting an acceptable bare except with a genuine defect, so the model learns the distinguishing property.
Add a `detected_pattern` field to each finding so you can analyze which code constructs developers dismiss most often and target those.

rationale.correct: The two accepted cases share a property — a deliberate, documented catch-all at a framework boundary — and few-shot examples that contrast this against a genuine defect teach that property. That generalizes to the next legitimate catch-all the codebase grows, which a hardcoded exception list cannot.

distractors.A: Path exclusions eliminate the specific false positives immediately and are simple to maintain, making this a practical option. They also blind the review to real defects elsewhere in those files, and every future deliberate bare except needs a new exclusion.
distractors.B: Naming the two locations in the prompt is targeted and would work for today's code. It encodes a file list rather than a principle, so it does not transfer, and the prompt accumulates special cases as the codebase evolves.
distractors.D: Instrumenting findings with `detected_pattern` is genuinely valuable and is the right way to analyze dismissal patterns systematically. It is a measurement mechanism rather than a fix — useful for finding which categories need attention, but it does not by itself change what gets flagged.

scenario: A support agent handles clear requests well but responds inconsistently to ambiguous ones — for example, "my order is wrong" with no order number, which could mean a wrong item, wrong quantity, or wrong address. Sometimes it asks a clarifying question, sometimes it guesses, sometimes it escalates.
stem: How should few-shot examples be constructed to help?

options.text: Two to four examples built around ambiguous requests, each showing why one action was chosen over the plausible alternatives.
Supply examples of the agent asking clarifying questions in every ambiguous case, establishing a consistent default.
Supply five to eight examples of well-formed requests handled correctly, so the model has a clear model of good behavior to imitate.
Supply one example per ambiguity type — wrong item, wrong quantity, wrong address — showing the correct handling for each.

rationale.correct: Few-shot examples are most valuable where the decision is genuinely hard, and the inconsistency is concentrated in ambiguous cases. A small number of examples targeting that ambiguity, each showing why the chosen action beat the plausible alternatives, teaches the discrimination rather than just the outcome.

distractors.B: Always asking a clarifying question is consistent and safe, which has real appeal. It is wrong in the cases where the agent could resolve the request directly, so it trades unpredictability for a uniform behavior that suppresses first-contact resolution.
distractors.C: Examples of well-formed requests are cheap to produce and demonstrate the desired tone and format. The agent already handles clear requests well, so these examples spend tokens on the behavior that is not broken and leave the ambiguous cases unaddressed.
distractors.D: Covering each ambiguity type is systematic and would help on those three, so the instinct is sound. It enumerates categories rather than teaching how to reason under uncertainty, so a fourth kind of ambiguity is unhandled — and showing the correct action without the reasoning gives the model less to generalize from.

scenario: You moved invoice extraction to `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema. JSON syntax errors and missing required fields are gone. Downstream accounting still rejects about 4% of records: line items that do not sum to the stated total, and tax amounts appearing in the shipping field.
stem: What does this tell you, and what should you add?

options.text: The tool description is unclear about field meanings; document each field precisely so the model stops confusing tax with shipping.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones; add `calculated_total` alongside `stated_total` and a `conflict_detected` flag.
The schema is under-constrained; add `minimum`/`maximum` bounds and stricter field types so invalid values cannot validate.
The extraction should switch from `tool_choice: "any"` to a forced tool call so the correct schema is always applied.

rationale.correct: Schema enforcement guarantees shape, not meaning. A tax amount placed in the shipping field is a well-typed number in a valid field, so no schema can catch it. Extracting a derived total alongside the stated one turns an invisible semantic error into a checkable discrepancy, and a conflict flag lets genuinely inconsistent sources be surfaced rather than silently resolved.

distractors.A: Clearer field documentation would reduce confusion between similar fields and is good practice. It lowers the error rate probabilistically rather than detecting errors when they occur, so records would still reach accounting uncaught, just somewhat less often.
distractors.C: Tighter bounds and types do catch a real class of errors and are worth having. Neither described failure violates any plausible bound — the misplaced tax amount is a legitimate positive number, and mis-summing line items are each individually valid — so this cannot close the gap.
distractors.D: Forcing a specific tool guarantees which schema is applied and matters when several extraction schemas exist. The scenario shows the right schema already being applied — the values within it are wrong — so this addresses a problem that is not occurring.

scenario: Your contract-extraction schema marks `governing_law` as required. Roughly 15% of contracts do not state a governing law. For those, the model returns plausible but fabricated values such as "State of Delaware," which pass validation and reach downstream systems.
stem: What is the correct schema change?

options.text: Keep the field required and add a separate `governing_law_confidence` number the downstream system can threshold on.
Keep the field required and instruct the model in the prompt to return the string `"NOT_FOUND"` when the contract does not state a governing law.
Keep the field required and add a retry that re-extracts whenever downstream review flags a suspicious value.
Make the field optional and nullable, giving the model a schema-valid way to report absence.

rationale.correct: A required field creates pressure to produce something, and fabrication is the predictable result when the information is genuinely absent. Making the field optional and nullable gives absence a first-class, schema-valid representation, which removes the incentive to invent a value.

distractors.A: A confidence field gives downstream systems a signal to act on and is genuinely useful for routing review. The fabricated value still enters the record, the model must still emit something for a required field, and self-reported confidence on a value it invented is unreliable.
distractors.B: A sentinel string is a recognizable pattern and would technically let the model signal absence, so this is a real option. It encodes a null through the type system's back door — every consumer must know to check for the magic value, and nothing prevents the model from returning a fabricated law instead, since both satisfy the schema equally.
distractors.C: Retrying on flagged values is reasonable when the failure is a format or structure problem. Retries cannot recover information that is not in the source document, so re-extraction will keep producing a fabricated value or fail repeatedly.

scenario: Your pipeline receives four document types and has a distinct extraction schema for each. Document type is not known before processing, and there is no reliable classifier upstream. Occasionally the model returns a conversational reply — "This appears to be an invoice, would you like me to extract it?" — instead of calling any extraction tool, which breaks the pipeline.
stem: What configuration addresses this?

options.text: Force a specific tool with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}` after adding a classification step to determine the document type.
Set `tool_choice: "auto"` and add a prompt instruction that the model must always call an extraction tool.
Merge the four schemas into one union schema and force that single tool on every document.
Set `tool_choice: "any"`, requiring a call to one of the four extraction tools while leaving the choice to the model.

rationale.correct: `"any"` is exactly this case: it guarantees a tool call rather than conversational text, while leaving the choice among the four schemas to the model. That matches a pipeline where the document type is unknown but some extraction must always occur.

distractors.A: Classify-then-force is a legitimate architecture and gives the strongest guarantee about which schema runs, so it is a defensible design. It adds a step and a round trip, and the scenario states no reliable classifier exists — so you would be building the missing component to solve a problem `"any"` already handles.
distractors.B: `"auto"` is the current permissive behavior and is what allows the conversational replies. Adding a prompt instruction makes compliance more likely but not guaranteed, which leaves the pipeline breaking intermittently.
distractors.C: A union schema with a forced tool does guarantee a call and simplifies selection to one tool, which has real appeal. It gives up the per-type validation that four distinct schemas provide, since a union must permit every type's fields, so much of the structural enforcement is lost.

scenario: Your extraction pipeline retries on any validation failure by resubmitting the same document and prompt. Analysis of retry outcomes: failures where a date was returned as `03/04/2024` instead of ISO 8601 succeed on retry about 80% of the time; failures where `beneficiary_ssn` is missing never succeed, because the SSN lives in a separate document the pipeline does not supply.
stem: How should the retry logic change?

options.text: Make `beneficiary_ssn` optional so those documents validate cleanly, and keep retrying the date format failures exactly as the pipeline does now.
Append the specific validation error to the retry prompt, and route failures caused by information absent from the source instead of retrying them.
Retry with a higher temperature so the model explores different interpretations of the document.
Cap retries at two attempts for all failure types, so the unrecoverable cases stop consuming budget.

rationale.correct: Two changes address the two observed classes. Resubmitting an identical prompt gives the model no new information, so including the specific validation error is what enables correction on format and structure failures. And retries cannot conjure data absent from the source, so those failures need routing — to a document-gathering step or human review — rather than repeated attempts.

distractors.A: Making the field optional is correct schema design when a value may legitimately be absent from the source, so half of this reflects sound reasoning. Here the SSN exists and simply is not being supplied — so marking it optional papers over a pipeline gap and produces records missing data the business needs, while the blind-retry problem persists.
distractors.C: Higher temperature increases variation and might occasionally stumble onto the right date format. It is a random search in place of a specific correction signal, it makes output less predictable, and no temperature can produce an SSN that is not in the document.
distractors.D: Capping attempts does bound the waste on unrecoverable cases and is a sensible guardrail to have. It treats both classes identically, so it still spends two attempts on every impossible extraction and does not improve the recoverable ones, which retry blindly rather than with feedback.

scenario: A Pydantic validator rejects an extracted purchase order because `line_items` sum to $4,820 while `stated_total` is $5,102. The source document is legible and contains both figures; the discrepancy exists in the original because a freight surcharge was omitted from the itemization.
stem: What should the pipeline do?

options.text: Retry with the validation error appended, so the model can correct the arithmetic.
Extract the discrepancy as data: record both figures, set a `conflict_detected` flag, and route for human review.
Fail the record and log it for manual re-keying, since automated extraction cannot resolve a contradictory source.
Relax the validator to permit a tolerance band, since small mismatches are common in real documents.

rationale.correct: The extraction is correct — both figures were read accurately — and the inconsistency is a property of the source document. Treating that as an extraction failure misattributes the problem. Capturing both values with an explicit conflict flag preserves what the document actually says and routes a genuine business question to someone who can resolve it.

distractors.A: Retrying with the error is the right response to a genuine extraction mistake, and the arithmetic mismatch looks like one. Here the model reported the document faithfully, so retrying pressures it to alter a correctly extracted figure to satisfy the validator — which would silently corrupt the record.
distractors.C: Failing loudly rather than guessing is defensible and better than silent corruption. It discards a complete, accurate extraction and forces full re-keying to resolve a single flagged question, which is far more expensive than surfacing the conflict on an otherwise good record.
distractors.D: A tolerance band is pragmatic and reflects that minor rounding differences are common in real documents. A $282 freight surcharge is not rounding noise, and a tolerance wide enough to absorb it would suppress real extraction errors, so it trades a visible discrepancy for silent data loss.

scenario: Developers dismiss roughly 40% of your review bot's findings. You have the dismissal counts per category but no insight into what the dismissed findings have in common, so prompt improvements have been guesswork.
stem: What instrumentation would most improve the feedback loop?

options.text: Track per-category dismissal rates over time and prioritize prompt work on whichever category trends worst.
Add a `detected_pattern` field recording the code construct that triggered each finding, so dismissals can be analyzed by construct.
Have the model attach a confidence score to each finding so you can check whether dismissals cluster at low confidence.
Add a free-text field where developers can explain each dismissal.

rationale.correct: You already know which categories are dismissed; the missing information is what the dismissed findings have in common. Recording the triggering construct on each finding makes that analyzable — patterns like "every dismissal in this category involves the retry decorator" become visible, which converts prompt improvement from guesswork into targeted work.

distractors.A: Trend tracking is useful for prioritization and requires no new instrumentation, so it is a reasonable operational addition. It refines information you already have — which category is worst — without revealing why, so prompt work stays guesswork within the chosen category.
distractors.C: Confidence scores would let you test whether dismissals correlate with low confidence, which is a legitimate diagnostic. Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is unreliable precisely on false positives, where the model is confidently wrong, so the correlation is likely to be weak and uninformative.
distractors.D: Developer explanations would be the richest signal available and directly answer why a finding was wrong. They depend on busy developers writing them, coverage is typically sparse and biased, and free text resists aggregation — so the systematic pattern stays hard to see.

scenario: A compliance workflow must return results within 30 hours of document arrival. Documents arrive continuously. You want the Message Batches API for its 50% savings, and batch processing can take up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency.
stem: What submission cadence guarantees the SLA with margin for submission and retrieval overhead?

options.text: Submit every 24 hours, since batches typically complete much faster than the ceiling and daily submission minimizes overhead.
Submit continuously as documents arrive, one batch per document, so queue wait is eliminated.
Submit every 6 hours: worst case a document waits 6 hours to be batched plus 24 hours of processing, totaling exactly 30.
Submit every 4 hours, leaving a 2-hour margin inside the 30-hour SLA after the 24-hour processing ceiling.

rationale.correct: The budget is queue wait plus processing. With a 24-hour processing ceiling against a 30-hour SLA, at most 6 hours may be spent waiting to be batched — and a document arriving just after a submission waits nearly the full window. A 4-hour cadence caps that wait at 4 hours, leaving margin for submission and retrieval overhead.

distractors.A: Daily submission does minimize operational overhead, and it is true that batches often finish well under the ceiling. Planning against typical rather than worst-case latency is exactly what an SLA forbids, and a 24-hour queue wait plus 24-hour processing is 48 hours in the worst case.
distractors.B: Per-document batches do eliminate queue wait and would meet the SLA. They forfeit the aggregation that makes batch processing operationally sensible, multiply request overhead, and each single-document batch is still subject to the same 24-hour ceiling — so there is no latency gain to offset the cost.
distractors.C: The arithmetic is right and this is the tempting answer: 6 plus 24 equals 30. It consumes the entire SLA with zero margin, so any submission delay, retrieval lag, or clock skew produces a breach — and a document arriving moments after a submission experiences essentially the full 6-hour wait.

scenario: You submit 500 documents to the Message Batches API. Twelve fail: eight because the document exceeded the context limit, four due to a transient service error. You have the batch results file and each request's `custom_id`.
stem: What is the correct recovery?

options.text: Resubmit only the twelve by `custom_id`, chunking the eight oversized documents and retrying the four transient failures unchanged.
Route the twelve failures to the synchronous API, which has different limits and will handle them without modification.
Resubmit the twelve failures unchanged, since transient errors resolve on retry and the oversized documents may succeed if the service is less loaded.
Resubmit the entire batch of 500, since partial resubmission risks inconsistent processing across the set.

rationale.correct: `custom_id` exists to correlate requests and responses, which is what makes selective resubmission possible. The two failure classes need different handling: oversized documents will fail identically until chunked, while transient errors are genuinely retryable as-is. Resubmitting only the twelve, appropriately modified, is the efficient and correct recovery.

distractors.B: Falling back to the synchronous API is a reasonable pattern for handling stragglers and would work for the transient failures. Context limits are a property of the model rather than the batch endpoint, so the oversized documents fail there too — and this forfeits the batch discount without solving the actual problem.
distractors.C: Retrying unchanged is correct for the four transient failures, and that partial correctness makes this attractive. The eight oversized documents exceed a hard limit, so they will fail identically on every retry regardless of service load — service load and context limits are unrelated.
distractors.D: Full resubmission does guarantee a uniform processing run and avoids any risk of mismatched results, which is a legitimate concern in some pipelines. It reprocesses 488 successful documents at full cost, and the eight oversized ones fail again anyway since nothing about them changed.

scenario: A proposed workflow uses the Message Batches API to run a multi-step research task: for each of 2,000 topics, search the web, read the top results, and produce a summary. The team's reasoning is that the work is latency-tolerant and runs overnight, so batching is the obvious cost win.
stem: What is the problem with this plan?

options.text: Batch requests cannot use tools at all, so no tool-based workflow is eligible.
Two thousand requests exceeds the practical size of a single batch and would need splitting.
Web search results would be up to 24 hours stale by the time the batch completes, so the summaries would reflect an outdated view of each topic.
The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a request, so it cannot execute a search and feed results back mid-request.

rationale.correct: The workload is genuinely latency-tolerant, so the team's cost reasoning is sound — the blocker is a capability limit. The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request, meaning it cannot execute a search, return results, and continue reasoning. The workflow must be restructured so tool execution happens outside the batched call.

distractors.A: This overstates the limitation. Tool definitions can be included in batch requests; what is unavailable is the multi-turn loop where results are executed and returned mid-request. The distinction matters, since single-turn tool use — such as forcing a structured-output extraction tool — remains a valid batch pattern.
distractors.B: Batch sizing is a legitimate operational concern and large jobs do sometimes need splitting. It is a mechanical constraint with an easy remedy, and 2,000 requests is not an unusual batch size, so it does not explain why the design fails.
distractors.C: Staleness is a real consideration for time-sensitive research and worth weighing in some designs. It presumes searches execute at submission time, which is not how this would work, and for most research topics a day of drift is immaterial — so this is a secondary concern rather than the blocker.

scenario: After generating a payment-reconciliation module, you append to the same session: "Now carefully review the code you just wrote and report any bugs." It reports no issues. QA later finds an off-by-one in a loop boundary that the model itself wrote. Repeating the request with stronger wording and with extended thinking enabled produces the same clean bill of health.
stem: What explains this and what is the fix?

options.text: The model retains its generation reasoning in-session and will not question it; use a second independent instance without that context.
The module is too large for a single review pass; splitting it into functions and reviewing each separately would catch the boundary error.
The review instruction is too general; asking for specific checks such as boundary conditions and off-by-one errors would surface it.
Extended thinking was not given enough budget to reconsider the loop logic thoroughly.

rationale.correct: Self-review in the same session is limited by construction: the reasoning that produced the off-by-one is still in context and still looks correct, so the model is reviewing its conclusion rather than the code. That neither stronger wording nor extended thinking helped is the signature of this blind spot. An independent instance without that reasoning context evaluates the code on its own terms.

distractors.B: Splitting large reviews into focused passes is the correct remedy for attention dilution across many files, and it is a real technique. A single module with one off-by-one is not an attention-dilution case, and each smaller pass in the same session carries the same generation context.
distractors.C: Specific review criteria genuinely improve review quality and would be worth adding to any review prompt. They do not remove the anchoring — the model would check boundary conditions and conclude, from the same reasoning that produced them, that they are right.
distractors.D: More thinking budget lets the model reason longer, which helps on genuinely hard problems. The scenario states extended thinking was already tried without effect, and more of the same reasoning does not escape an anchor built into the context.

scenario: Your review produces useful findings, but reviewers cannot tell which deserve careful attention and which are speculative, so they read all of them at equal depth and the bot's throughput advantage is lost.
stem: What addition most improves review routing?

options.text: Group findings by category so reviewers can process similar issues together.
Run a verification pass in which the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding, so review attention can be routed.
Report only findings the model would classify as high severity, suppressing the rest.
Have the model rank all findings against one another and present them in priority order, so reviewers work down the list from most to least important.

rationale.correct: A verification pass that attaches self-reported confidence to each finding gives reviewers a signal for allocating attention — read the uncertain ones closely, skim the confident ones. That is the recognized use of self-reported confidence in multi-pass review: routing effort, not making automated accept/reject decisions.

distractors.A: Category grouping is a genuine ergonomic improvement and reduces context switching for reviewers. It reorganizes the same undifferentiated list, so reviewers still cannot tell which items within a category warrant scrutiny.
distractors.C: Suppressing lower-severity findings would cut volume immediately and is tempting under throughput pressure. Severity and reliability are different axes — a low-severity finding can be certainly correct and a high-severity one speculative — so this discards real issues while leaving the confidence question unanswered.
distractors.D: Relative ranking does impose an order and would help reviewers start with the most important items, so it is a reasonable alternative. A rank position carries no information about whether a finding is likely correct, and forcing a total order across unrelated findings creates false precision between items that are not comparable.

scenario: You are designing review for a service where an agent both generates migration scripts and must catch defects before they run against production. You have budget for two model passes per script.
stem: How should the two passes be allocated?

options.text: One generation pass, then one pass that re-runs generation from scratch and diffs the two outputs.
One generation pass, then a second pass in the same session asking the model to critique its own work with specific checks.
Two independent generation passes, shipping the script only where both agree.
One generation pass, then one review pass by an independent instance without the generator's reasoning context.

rationale.correct: With exactly two passes, the second is most valuable as an independent review: an instance without the generator's reasoning context evaluates the script on its own merits and is substantially better at catching subtle defects than same-session self-review.

distractors.A: Generate-and-diff is a real technique and divergences do flag genuinely uncertain regions, so this is a defensible use of the second pass. It surfaces only disagreement, so a defect both passes make consistently — the most likely kind, since they share a prompt and model — goes unflagged, and someone must still adjudicate every benign stylistic difference.
distractors.B: Same-session self-critique with specific checks is better than an unstructured self-review and costs nothing extra to set up. It still leaves the generation reasoning in context, which is the limitation that makes self-review weak — so it spends the second pass on the least effective option available.
distractors.C: Agreement between two independent generations offers some assurance and is a recognizable ensembling idea. Two runs of the same model on the same prompt correlate strongly in their mistakes, so common defects survive, and the scheme has no mechanism for reviewing the agreed output.

scenario: A long support conversation uses progressive summarization to stay within budget. Early in the conversation the customer stated order #4471, a $128.40 disputed charge, and a promised delivery date of March 3. Forty turns later the agent tells the customer "we'll refund the amount in question for your recent order," having lost the specific figures to summarization.
stem: What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Stop summarizing and pass the complete conversation history on every request so no detail is ever lost.
Place the earliest turns at the end of the prompt so the original figures land in the high-recall tail rather than the middle.
Instruct the summarizer to preserve all numbers, dates, and identifiers verbatim when condensing.
Extract transactional facts into a persistent "case facts" block included in every prompt, kept outside the summarized history.

rationale.correct: Summarization is lossy by design, so the durable fix is to remove critical facts from its scope entirely. A persistent case-facts block holds the identifiers, amounts, and dates as structured data included in every prompt, so they survive regardless of how aggressively the conversational history is condensed.

distractors.A: Full history guarantees nothing is lost and is the simplest correct-by-construction option, which is why it appeals. It is exactly what the token budget forbids in a forty-turn conversation, and unbounded growth eventually forces truncation anyway — usually of the oldest turns, where these facts live.
distractors.B: Position-aware ordering is a real technique for mitigating lost-in-the-middle effects and is worth applying to long aggregated inputs. The figures here were removed by summarization rather than under-attended, so reordering what remains cannot recover them.
distractors.C: Instructing the summarizer to retain numbers verbatim is a sensible and cheap improvement that would help in many turns. It keeps the critical facts inside the lossy channel, so compliance is probabilistic and degrades as the history grows and each successive summary summarizes a summary.

scenario: A synthesis agent receives aggregated findings from four subagents as one long input. Its reports consistently reflect the first and last subagents' contributions well, while the middle two are underrepresented — even though all four returned substantive, comparable findings. Rotating which subagent appears in which position moves the problem rather than fixing it.
stem: What is the most effective mitigation?

options.text: Instruct the synthesis agent to give equal weight to all four subagents' findings.
Sort the findings by relevance score so the most important material occupies the beginning and end regardless of source.
Split synthesis into four passes, one per subagent, then combine the four partial syntheses.
Lead with a consolidated key-findings summary and organize the detailed results under explicit section headers.

rationale.correct: That rotation moves rather than fixes the problem confirms a position effect rather than a content difference. Leading with a key-findings summary puts every contribution in the high-attention opening, and explicit section headers give the detailed material structure the model can navigate, which is the standard mitigation for long aggregated inputs.

distractors.A: An equal-weight instruction is cheap and expresses the desired outcome directly. Position effects are not a matter of intent, so instructing the model to attend evenly does not change how a long undifferentiated input is actually processed.
distractors.B: Relevance sorting is a reasonable use of position and ensures the most important material is well attended. It concedes that middle content will be underweighted rather than mitigating it, so lower-ranked-but-relevant findings are still lost — and it presumes relevance scores that are themselves reliable.
distractors.C: Per-subagent passes do guarantee each contribution gets full attention, which makes this a serious option. Synthesis is precisely the act of relating findings across sources, so partial syntheses computed in isolation cannot surface cross-source agreement, conflict, or convergence — and combining them reintroduces the same aggregation problem one level up.

scenario: A downstream report-generation agent has a tight context budget. Its upstream analysis agent currently returns full reasoning chains and long verbatim excerpts. The report agent needs the conclusions, the supporting citations, and a sense of how well-supported each conclusion is.
stem: What change to the upstream agent best fits the constraint?

options.text: Keep the current output and have the report agent summarize it on receipt before generating.
Have the upstream agent return structured data — key facts, citations, support scores — instead of verbose content and reasoning chains.
Keep the current output but truncate it to the first N tokens that fit the report agent's budget.
Have the report agent request the upstream output in pieces across several turns, assembling the report incrementally as each piece arrives.

rationale.correct: When a downstream agent has a limited context budget, the upstream agent should return structured data rather than verbose prose. Key facts, citations, and support scores are exactly what the report agent needs, delivered in a fraction of the tokens, and the structure preserves the citation bindings that matter for the report.

distractors.A: Summarizing on receipt does compress the input and is a natural instinct. The verbose output must first fit in the report agent's context to be summarized, which is the constraint being violated, and summarizing prose is where citation-to-claim bindings typically get lost.
distractors.C: Truncation fits the budget by construction and is trivial to implement. It discards content arbitrarily, so whichever conclusions and citations fall past the cutoff simply vanish, with no relationship between what is kept and what matters.
distractors.D: Chunked multi-turn retrieval does bound per-turn context and is a legitimate pattern for large inputs. It adds round trips and leaves the report agent unable to see all conclusions at once when deciding structure and emphasis, which is central to writing a coherent report.

scenario: A customer opens with: "This is the third time I've contacted you about this. I want to speak to a manager." The underlying issue is a duplicate charge, which your agent is fully capable of refunding autonomously.
stem: What should the agent do?

options.text: Investigate the duplicate charge and resolve it, then offer to connect the customer to a manager if they still want one after seeing it fixed.
Investigate the charge and gather the order details first so the handoff summary is complete, then escalate with that summary attached.
Escalate to a human immediately, since the customer has explicitly requested one.
Acknowledge the frustration and ask whether the customer would prefer the agent resolve the charge now or wait for a manager.

rationale.correct: An explicit request for a human is an escalation trigger in its own right and should be honored immediately, without first attempting investigation. The agent's capability to resolve the issue does not override a clearly stated preference, particularly on a third contact where prior attempts have already failed the customer.

distractors.A: Resolving first and offering the manager afterward maximizes first-contact resolution and would satisfy many customers. It substitutes the agent's judgment for a clearly stated preference, which is the behavior that turns a solvable complaint into a serious one.
distractors.B: A complete, well-researched handoff is genuinely good practice and would produce the best-informed escalation, which makes this the closest alternative. It delays an explicit request for a human in order to build a case file — the escalation should carry what is already known rather than pausing to gather more.
distractors.D: Acknowledging frustration while offering resolution is the correct pattern when a customer expresses anger without explicitly demanding a human. Here the request is unambiguous, so re-asking reads as deflection and adds friction on a third contact.

scenario: A customer asks you to match a competitor's lower price. Your published policy covers price adjustments for items that drop in price on your own site within 14 days. It says nothing at all about competitor pricing — the situation is neither permitted nor prohibited. The agent currently declines, citing the 14-day own-site policy.
stem: What should the agent do instead?

options.text: Decline but offer the own-site adjustment if the item's price drops within 14 days, resolving what policy does cover.
Escalate: the policy is silent on this request, and a policy gap is an escalation trigger distinct from case complexity.
Decline, since anything not explicitly permitted by policy should be treated as not permitted.
Approve the match, since nothing in the policy prohibits it and approving preserves first-contact resolution.

rationale.correct: Policy gaps and exceptions are escalation triggers in their own right, separate from case complexity. The policy neither permits nor prohibits competitor matching, so the agent has no basis for either answer, and someone with authority to set precedent should decide. Citing an unrelated own-site rule as though it settled the question is the current defect.

distractors.A: Offering the adjustment that policy does cover is genuinely good service and worth doing alongside the escalation. As a complete response it still resolves the gap by declining, so the agent has silently decided an open policy question while appearing helpful.
